Some live feeds don't answer a poll: vessel positions, market ticks and alert streams arrive as a WebSocket or a server-sent event stream that pushes messages while it is open and keeps no cursor, so whatever arrives while you are disconnected is gone. The hub's sources today are calls it makes (#364), a cursor stream that loses nothing across a restart, and MCP tools (#261). A pushed feed fits none of them: it can't promise no loss, and a message a second per entity is too many to record one at a time. Add a pushed source kind that the hub holds open, folds into windows, records as one batch a window, and marks honestly: every reconnect is a recorded gap, every drop is counted, and values not heard since a gap go stale on their own freshness.

**Runs on:** Any machine; every criterion runs against local test servers on a test clock.

### Scope
- A source may declare `push: ws {url} | sse {url}`, on a host its grant names, with its secret by handle in a header as for any source (never in the URL). The hub opens it while something binds the source and is shown, or while a schedule or notice needs it, and closes it otherwise, as `while_shown` does.
- Fold: messages are parsed by the source's schema into rows of a data layout (at most 64 bytes a row) keyed by a field, and folded into a window of `every` (at least 1 s): `latest` keeps each key's last row in the window, `append` keeps every row. At the window's end the hub records one `reading.batch` event with the window's rows as one evidence file, the window's as-of time and its counts (messages, rows, dropped). A window may hold up to 65,536 rows; rows past that are dropped and counted, never silently.
- A message that doesn't match the schema makes no row and is counted as refused, with its first 200 bytes kept, secrets scrubbed, for the source's panel. A message whose own time is later than its arrival is refused, as for any reading.
- Gaps: a disconnect, a close, a missed heartbeat (`heartbeat: s`) or a hub restart records `push.gap {from, to, cause}`. Reconnects back off from 1 s to 60 s with jitter, within the source's quota of connects a minute. A server's snapshot on connect is folded like any message. Nothing claims the stream lost no data: a batch says what it received, a gap says when nothing could be received, and a key not heard since a gap goes stale on its own freshness.
- Keeping: a pushed source declares `keep: {full: h ≤ 24, thinned: d ≤ 7, every: s}`. Windows older than `full` are thinned to one row a key every `every` seconds, older than `thinned` dropped, unless a check or an ask cites them. Batches count toward the record's size budget, and a source whose rate would pass its share is refused at install, naming the estimate.
- A piece and a view read a pushed source as they read any series or row reading: at the frame's pinned log position, so a replay reads the windows the live view read. Replay with a clock replays recorded windows and gaps, never the network.

### Fields
**Source (amended)**
- `push: ws {url, subprotocol} | sse {url} | none = none`; `heartbeat: s | none`; `fold: {key: field, mode: latest | append, every: s ≥ 1, layout: name@version}`; `keep: {full: h, thinned: d, every: s}`; quota adds `connects_per_minute`
- Events: `reading.batch` adds `{messages, rows, dropped, refused}`; new `push.gap {source, from, to, cause: closed | error | heartbeat | restart | quota}`
- It can never: Record a message one event at a time; claim a window complete across a gap; put a secret in a URL; keep a stream open with nothing bound and shown and no schedule or notice needing it; drop a row without counting it

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A local WebSocket server sends 12,000 keyed position messages a second for 60 s; with `fold: latest, every: 5 s` the hub records 12 batch events, each with at most 12,000 rows and its message count, and nothing else in the record for those messages; a planted hub that records one event per message fails, naming the event count
- [ ] An SSE server sending 50 events a second with `fold: append, every: 1 s` records 50 rows a batch; with the test server pausing 30 s and resuming, the record holds one `push.gap` of 30 s, cause `heartbeat` with `heartbeat: 10 s`, and a key not heard since turns stale at its freshness
- [ ] A window of 70,000 rows records 65,536 and `dropped: 4,464`; a message with a missing key field records no row and `refused: 1`, its first 200 bytes kept with the secret's three encodings scrubbed
- [ ] A server that closes the connection every 5 s is reconnected with backoff 1, 2, 4 … 60 s with jitter, never past `connects_per_minute`, and each close is a gap with cause `closed`
- [ ] With no view showing the source and no schedule or notice needing it, the connection closes within 10 s, and reopens when a view binding it is shown; a planted host that holds it open fails, naming the source
- [ ] The source's key is sent in a header the source names and appears in no URL, log, trace or record, in any of its encodings
- [ ] After `full` = 1 h, windows thin to one row a key every 60 s, and a window a check cites stays whole; a source whose declared rate × row size would pass its record share is refused at install, naming the estimate
- [ ] A recorded hour with two gaps, replayed on a test clock with the network off, gives the same batches, gaps and stale values at every frame as the live run read
- [ ] Budgets, on the reference Mac in the local preflight, compared with the merge base: 12,000 messages a second folded into 5 s windows cost the hub under 5% of one core and add under 3 ms to its event loop's p99
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of the source's panel during a gap, after a reconnect and with refused messages listed, taken by the check run from the app, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it

### Proof
Recorded runs against local WebSocket and SSE test servers on a test clock: batch and gap counts, drops and refusals, backoff timings, open and close by what is shown, secret scans, thinning, replay with the network off, and the budget runs beside the merge base. Planted wrong programs that must fail: one event per message, a window claimed complete across a gap, a held-open stream, a key in a URL.

Sending messages to a pushed source beyond its subscribe message; WebTransport and raw TCP; ordering across two sources; a cursor or resume that a server doesn't offer.

Let you select lines in a session's changes and leave a note that reaches the session once, and close it only on proof: a later change to those lines whose checks pass, or you.

**Epic:** #241 · **Design:** [Sessions that know about each other](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#sessions-that-know-about-each-other) · [States people see](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#states-people-see)

### Scope
- In a session's Changes tab (#578), selecting a line range and typing writes a note as you, by your gesture: `{note, session, path, side, start, end, base, head, text}`, anchored to the base and head commits it was written against
- The note reaches the session once, by the adapter's delivery route a note on its row takes (#329). The lines go in a separate field, marked as data, never as your words
- The note shows beside its lines, and on that session's later return cards with what keeps it open. It closes only when a later change touches those lines and the checks covering that path pass, or when you close it. No agent or plug-in can write, edit or close one
- An agent's reply about a note shows beside it, marked as the agent's words. A reply never closes the note
- If its lines no longer exist after a rebase or deletion, the note reads `detached` with the commit that removed them. A note never opens an ask or adds to the count
- There's one gesture. Lines selected in Changes attach to the page's box, as any pointing does (#807). What's sent with lines attached shows beside those lines and is a note: open until a passing change or you close it. It adds no second field and no mode
- A line note can't be `note.opened@1`, whose data requires `doc`, `item`, `rev` and `region`. It is recorded as a new version of `note.opened` whose data holds either that item anchor or the line anchor `{session, path, side, start, end, base, head}`. Version 1's schema and digest stay as they are, and the `notes` projection reads both versions

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Selecting lines 12-18 of cart/total.ts in a fixture session's Changes tab and typing "round before tax" delivers one message to the session, with the words and a separate `{path, side, start, end, base, head}` attachment, and records `note.opened`. A planted tab that pastes the lines into your words fails, naming the note
- [ ] The agent replies "done" with no change to those lines. The note stays open, and the reply shows marked as the agent's. A planted host that closes a note on the agent's reply fails, naming the note
- [ ] A later commit that changes lines 12-18, with the covering cart check passing, closes the note with `{by: check, rev, run}`. The same change with that check failing leaves it open. A planted host that closes on any change to the file fails, naming the note
- [ ] A test agent's attempt to write or close a note through MCP is refused with `not_your_layer`. A rebase that deletes the lines shows the note `detached` with the commit
- [ ] A note adds nothing to the one count and fires no notification. A planted note that adds to Needs you fails, naming the surface
- [ ] With lines selected, the tree holds one text field, the box. A planted Changes view with its own note field fails, naming it
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of a note beside its lines in the Changes tab, open, closed by a passing change and detached, taken by the check run from the app at the reference window, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it
- [ ] The fixture line note's `note.opened` validates against its new version's published schema, and `note.opened@1`'s digest is unchanged. A planted line note written as `note.opened@1` fails the contract check, naming `doc`

### Proof
The fixture session's note delivered, kept open past the agent's "done", closed by a passing change, and detached by a rebase, each planted host shown failing.

A live 3D warehouse made by Claude Code from a library of thousands of industrial models and run end to end. Six reach trucks put pallets away into three rows of racks and bring them to two pick-and-pack lines on roller conveyors, which feed outbound doors where trailers load. The trucks keep to the painted lanes, wait at junctions and park in their bays when idle. A bar across the top shows orders per hour, order-to-ship time, rack fill and free forklifts. Click a forklift, a line or a door and the camera follows it, with a card of its live numbers. You can pause it, run it at 1×, 2×, 5× or 10× against its clock, and open it from a link in a browser. The agent writes the piece, the app plays it, and the checks pass it on evaluated data: every number on screen is read from the running model.

A warehouse, a factory line, a clinic or a call center shown as a live model is a process: work arrives, waits in queues, holds resources for a while, rides conveyors, gets packed into batches and leaves, and the screen shows throughput, time in system and how busy each resource is. Today a piece writes all of that in its own logic, unproven. A case can vanish between a belt and a pallet, a forklift can count as free while it carries a load, and "orders per hour" can disagree with the orders that left. This adds `process@1`, a first-party library interface with a reference library, and three kind rules that hold any library under it to what a process must keep: nothing made or lost without a source or an exit, a resource busy exactly while something holds it, and Little's law over each station. It's a library a piece links, like `mods.lib@1` (#953), not a genre kit, so it waits on no kit.

**Epic:** #219 · **Design:** [Library interfaces](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#library-interfaces) · [Logic: library interfaces](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#logic-library-interfaces) · [Logic: linked libraries](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#logic-linked-libraries) · [Pack: kind rules and the kind kit](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#pack-kind-rules-and-the-kind-kit) · [Honest numbers](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#honest-numbers)

### Scope
- Entities are rows with a kind (such as order, case or pallet), a generation, the step they were made, and where they are: a queue, a resource, a conveyor, a batch or out. A reused row takes a new generation, so a stale reference never finds the new entity.
- Sources make entities on a schedule: a fixed interval, a table of times, or gaps drawn from an exponential with the logic item's seeded random numbers. A sink takes an entity out and records its time in system.
- Queues are first in, first out, or ordered by a column, with an optional capacity. A full queue blocks whatever feeds it.
- Resources have a capacity, such as six forklifts, twelve pickers or four dock doors. A request is granted in step order, then by entity ID, so the same run grants the same way. Each resource keeps its busy count every step.
- Conveyors have a length, a speed and a minimum spacing. Items ride at the belt's speed and close up behind a blocked end, and the library writes each item's distance along the belt for drawing on a path.
- Batches pack n entities into one (cases onto a pallet, pallets into a trailer) and unpack them. A batch carries its members, and they come out unchanged.
- Statistics are arrays any bound value reads: throughput over a sliding window, time in system (mean and 90th percentile), queue lengths, busy counts and work in progress, per station and in all.
- Kind rules (#202), in the interface's pack:
  - `process.conserve`: at every step and for each kind, entities made equal entities in queues, resources, conveyors and batches plus entities out. A fail names the step, the kind and the gap.
  - `process.busy`: at every step, each resource's busy count equals the entities holding it and never passes its capacity.
  - `process.little`: over a declared window past the warm-up, each station's mean work in progress equals its throughput times its mean time in system, within the tolerance.
- Fixtures from first principles, and a planted library that drops an item when a belt blocks, which must fail `process.conserve`.

### Fields
- Interface `process@1`: exports `source`, `queue`, `resource`, `request`, `release`, `conveyor`, `pack`, `unpack`, `sink` and `stats`; layout `process.state@1` (entity rows, queue rings, resource holders, belt slots, statistics arrays)
- `source {kind, every: s | at: table ID | mean_gap: s, until: s (optional)}`; `queue {order: fifo | column, capacity: u32 (optional)}`; `resource {capacity: u16}`; `conveyor {length: m, speed: m/s, spacing: m, path: path ID (optional)}`; `pack {n: u16, into: kind}`; `stats {window: s = 3600, warmup: s = 0}`
- Kind rules: `process.conserve`, `process.busy`, `process.little {tolerance: f64 = 0.02 relative}`
- It can never: Make or drop an entity outside a source or a sink; grant past a resource's capacity; move an item through a blocked belt end; read the wall clock or an unseeded random number

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One source every 60 s into one resource of capacity 1 that holds each entity 45 s, at a 1/60 s step: over 10 simulated hours the busy share is 0.75 exactly, nothing ever waits, every time in system is 45 s, and `process.little` passes with mean work in progress 0.75.
- [ ] One source with exponential gaps at a mean of 2 min into one resource that holds each entity for an exponential time with a mean of 1 min, seeded, over 100,000 arrivals: the mean time in system is within 5% of 2 min and the mean work in progress within 5% of 1, and the same seed gives the same statistics arrays byte for byte.
- [ ] A conveyor 10 m long at 0.5 m/s with 0.6 m spacing carries a lone case end to end in 20 s. With its end blocked it holds 17 cases, the 18th waits at the infeed, and `process.conserve` passes at every step.
- [ ] Two resources of capacity 1 and three requests at the same step: the two lowest entity IDs are granted, the third waits and is granted at the step the first release happens. `process.busy` passes at every step.
- [ ] Six cases packed onto a pallet, the pallet carried through a queue and unpacked, give back the same six entities with their generations, and `process.conserve` holds while they're packed.
- [ ] The planted library that drops a case when the belt end blocks fails `process.conserve`, naming the step, the kind and a gap of 1. A planted library that grants a third request on a resource of capacity 2 fails `process.busy`, naming the resource and the step. The interface's pack is refused without its planted library.
- [ ] A bound value reading throughput over the last hour equals the count of sink records in that window at 20 sampled times. A planted label typed as "46" fails honest numbers (#406), naming the item.
- [ ] The reference library links only after every fixture passes on this core and in headless Chrome with the same step hashes (#531).
- [ ] Budget, a proposal until measured on the reference Mac in the local preflight: a model of 2,000 live entities, 40 queues, 30 resources and 10 conveyors steps in under 0.3 ms a step.
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of a warehouse model with queues, a resource and a conveyor and its throughput readout, taken by the check run from the canvas's own frames, with a recording of the model running, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it

### Proof
The fixtures' expected values with how each was worked out, the step hashes on this core and in headless Chrome, the check record for each kind rule, and the planted libraries' fails.

### Not in scope
Continuous flows of liquid or bulk material; optimizing a schedule; shifts and calendars beyond a table of source times.

Each look proof already drops candidates that are near-copies of each other, but nothing stops it offering the look you accepted last week, and the week before. Every piece then looks fine on its own and the same as the rest. Keep the looks of your recent pieces out of a look proof's candidates, by the same near-copy rule, unless the brief names that look.

**Epic:** #310 · **Design:** [Films and figures on the canvas](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#films-and-figures-on-the-canvas) · [Film brief: defaults, treatment and asks](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#film-brief-defaults-treatment-and-asks) · [Sheet `sheet@1`](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#sheet-sheet1) · [Ask](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#ask)

### Scope
- Recent looks: the looks of the last six look proofs you answered with a look, across every project on this machine, read from the record by the answer's time; each is a look asset by hash
- Before a look proof is asked, each recent look is rendered on the same moment's still as the candidates, and a candidate that counts as one with a recent look under the near-copy rule (OKLab ΔE under 0.1 at the 90th percentile of pixels, at the cell's size, on one machine) is replaced by another look that counts as one with neither the other candidates nor a recent look
- The replaced candidate is listed in the ask's existing `dropped: [{option, same_as}]`, with `same_as` naming the recent look's hash and the piece it came from; no new surface is drawn
- A look the brief names, or one a standing rule for the project names, is never replaced and never excluded
- When the looks on offer can't fill three candidates that keep clear of every recent look, the oldest recent look stops counting first, one at a time, and the ask's record lists each one that stopped counting
- The same record and brief give the same candidates

### Fields
**[Film brief: defaults, treatment and asks](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#film-brief-defaults-treatment-and-asks)**
- `look_proof: {recent: u8 = 6, scope: machine}` (the looks of the last `recent` answered look proofs, read from the record)
- `ask.created`'s `dropped: [{option, same_as}]`, where `same_as` may name `{look: hash, piece}` from the record
- It can never: Replace a look the brief or a standing rule names; count the agent's choice of a look, only your answer to a look proof; read anything but the record and the look assets; change after the ask is shown.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With six answered look proofs in the record, whose looks are clean, chalk, dark math, notebook and two others, a new brief whose drafter offers chalk among its three candidates shows three candidates none of which counts as one with any of the six, and the ask's dropped lists chalk with `same_as` naming the earlier piece; a planted drafter that ignores the record shows chalk and fails, naming it
- [ ] A look from the seventh most recent answered proof is offered when the drafter picks it
- [ ] A brief that names chalk gets chalk as a candidate, never replaced
- [ ] A recent look from another project on this machine is kept out the same way
- [ ] With only five looks on offer and six recent ones, the proof still shows three candidates, the record lists the oldest recent looks that stopped counting, in age order, and no candidate counts as one with a recent look that still counts
- [ ] The boundary pair: a candidate whose still differs from a recent look's still by ΔE 0.099 at the 90th percentile is replaced, and one at 0.101 is kept
- [ ] Asking the same brief twice against the same record shows the same three candidates
- [ ] A look the agent used without a look proof, in a piece you never answered, doesn't count as recent
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of a look proof's three candidates beside the recent looks they avoid, taken by the check run from the app at the reference window, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it

A requirement whose base fails only some of the time is proven by running its check on the base until one run fails at a named assertion, up to the count its declared rate needs, and passes only with that many clean runs on the claim's commit.

**Epic:** #3 · **Design:** [How runs become one of five verdicts](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#how-runs-become-one-of-five-verdicts) · [What done means, fixed at the start](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#what-done-means-fixed-at-the-start)

### Scope
- A definition may declare `on_base: fails_sometimes {rate}` for a requirement, the share of base runs that fail; the rate is part of the locked definition, so neither the agent nor the claim changes it
- The check runs on the base up to n = ceil(ln(0.05) ÷ ln(1 − rate)) times, stopping at the first run that fails on an assertion its check names, which proves the fix
- n base runs with no such failure make the check INVALID, naming the rate and the runs
- On the claim's commit the same check needs n clean runs, as any check that may be flaky does
- The drafting job's own base run uses the same count for such a requirement
- The rate is a field of the locked definition's requirement, a number above 0 and below 1, present only when `on_base` is `fails_sometimes`. `definition.locked@9` closes its requirement object and has no such field, so this task adds the next major of `definition.locked` and its generated types

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A fixture test that fails at its named assertion on about 30% of base runs, from a seeded race, with `on_base: fails_sometimes {rate: 0.3}`: the base runs stop at the first failing run, never more than 9 (ceil(ln 0.05 ÷ ln 0.7)), and the fix is proven, with each base run's outcome in the record
- [ ] The same requirement against a base where the race can't happen: 9 base runs pass and the check is INVALID, naming the rate 0.3 and the 9 runs
- [ ] A claim that only halves the failure rate: among the 9 runs on its commit at least one fails in the fixture's seeded schedule, and the verdict is not PASS
- [ ] The real fix passes 9 clean runs on the claim's commit and the requirement reads PASS
- [ ] A base run that fails only elsewhere, such as at an import, counts toward the 9 but proves nothing
- [ ] A claim whose diff changes the declared rate is refused, naming the definition's hash
- [ ] A requirement with plain `on_base: fails` still runs once on the base, unchanged

### Proof
The record of each base and head run with its outcome and where it failed, the locked definition with its rate, and the verdicts. A runner that stops after one passing base run, or that takes the rate from the claim, must fail.

- [ ] "use option B" sent as a note to the Claude Code session closes its choice ask as answered from the app, its card leaves Needs you, and the agent gets the words once; a host that delivers the words and leaves the choice open, so its card asks again, fails this test, naming the ask

- [ ] Pause on the Codex row denies its next tool call with your reason until you resume, and the agent's transcript shows the reason

You asked to start work from the app without setting up a folder by hand. Give each session the main box starts a worktree of its own, on a new branch from the default branch, owned by its task until the task settles and you remove it.

**Epic:** #241 · **Design:** [Starting a session from the app](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#start) · [Sessions that know about each other](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#sessions-that-know-about-each-other) · [Threats, and what stops each one](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#threats-and-what-stops-each-one)

### Scope
- A session started from the main box, or with New worktree picked on its start card (#574), gets a worktree of its own; one started from a session's page without it works in that session's worktree under path leases, as now
- Through paseo, the worktree is paseo's own worktree workspace; on DeepBuild's own route, the hub runs `git worktree add` through the supervisor, off its event loop, against the repo's own checkout, into `~/.deepbuild/worktrees/<repo>/<task>`, on a new branch from the remote-tracking default branch as last fetched
- It never fetches on its own: the start card says how old the last fetch is, and a stale base is recorded on the receipt, not refused
- `worktree.created` names the task as the worktree's owner, with its base commit; the session's page shows the worktree and branch
- The session takes its own leases there: ports per worktree as env-local leases them, and paths under path leases, as a child in a worktree of its own does
- DeepBuild never runs git inside an existing worktree and touches no other worktree's index or files
- A worktree goes only after its task has settled (merged, kept or released) and you press Remove on its row, recorded as `worktree.removed`; nothing removes it on its own, and one with uncommitted edits or commits on no remote branch can't be removed there, its row saying why
- On DeepBuild's own route, a new worktree starts with the local files git leaves out that the repo lists in `.worktreeinclude`, Claude Code's own file with gitignore patterns. They are cloned copy-on-write from the repo's own checkout before the session starts. A file is copied only when it is listed, gitignored, and inside the repo; a link is never followed out of it; an existing file is never overwritten; with no `.worktreeinclude`, nothing is copied. `worktree.created` names the files and never holds their contents. A listed file that isn't there is one reading on the session's page. The copies go with the worktree at Remove. A check's temporary checkout gets none of them
- Remove is on the session's page, under Where it runs (#578), and in the Session menu. Before it removes, it says what goes: the folder, and how many files in it git doesn't track. With none, it removes with no question. With some, it asks once, naming the count and the largest three. The branch stays, and on macOS the folder goes to the Trash

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] From the main box, "fix the flaky checkout test" with checkout-web as its repo starts its session in a new worktree under `~/.deepbuild/worktrees/checkout-web/`, on a new branch from `origin/main` as last fetched, and its row names the worktree and branch; a box that starts it in the repo's own checkout fails this test, naming the path
- [ ] The repo's worktree list gains exactly one entry, and no other worktree's HEAD, index or files change, by digests taken before and after; a trace of the hub's processes finds `git worktree add` started by the supervisor and no git command with another worktree as its folder
- [ ] With the last fetch three days old, the start card says how old it is and the session starts on that base, and its receipt names the base and how far behind the default branch it was
- [ ] Through paseo, the worktree is paseo's own workspace, recorded once as `worktree.created` with the task as owner; a second record of the same path fails this test, naming it
- [ ] Two sessions started from the main box in one repo each lease their own web port for their own worktree; a start that reuses the source checkout's port lease fails this test, naming the lease
- [ ] A settled task's worktree stays until you press Remove, and then `worktree.removed` is recorded; one with an unpushed commit can't be removed and its row says "unpushed commit, kept"; a cleanup that removes it fails this test, naming the commit
- [ ] Budgets (targets, to be measured), on the reference Mac in the local preflight, compared with the merge base: making the worktree adds under 2 s to a session's start on the fixture repo
- [ ] With `.env` gitignored and listed, and `secret.txt` gitignored and not listed, a new worktree holds `.env` byte for byte and no `secret.txt`, and `worktree.created` names only `.env`, with none of its contents. A start that copies every gitignored file fails this test, naming `secret.txt`
- [ ] A listed link that points at a file outside the repo, and a pattern `../x`, copy nothing and each raises one reading naming it
- [ ] With no `.worktreeinclude`, the worktree holds no gitignored file
- [ ] A check's temporary checkout for that session holds no `.env`; a checkout that copies it fails this test, naming the file
- [ ] A listed 2 GB file adds under 200 ms to the start on the reference Mac, with free disk unchanged by more than 1 MB (drafted budget, compared with the merge base)
- [ ] A settled worktree holding an ignored database file asks once, naming it, and after the yes the file is in the Trash. A planted Remove that deletes it with no question fails, naming the file. A worktree with no untracked file removes with no question

### Proof
A session started from the main box through paseo and one on DeepBuild's own route, each in its own worktree with the other worktrees' digests unchanged, and a settled task's worktree removed only after your press.

Notes you leave on an item of a document a card shows, sent to its writer as one send-back item and closed only by a passing revision or by you, and agent HTML deliverables opened in a wrapper with no network.

**Epic:** #241 · **Part of:** #145 · **Design:** [Threats, and what stops each one](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#threats-and-what-stops-each-one) · [Note](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#note)

### Scope
- An HTML deliverable opens inside a wrapper page DeepBuild writes, whose policy blocks every network request and allows only inline scripts, styles and data URLs, in a sandboxed frame with no same-origin access, and the app shows its source
- Notes (`note`): on a document a return card shows, you can leave a note on an item, written as you by your click in the card; it reaches the item's writer as one structured send-back item `{note, doc, item, rev, t, region, text}`, shows on that writer's later return cards with what keeps it open, and closes only when a later revision changes that item and the document's checks pass on it with every issue counted, or when you close it; no agent or plug-in can write, edit or close one, a note on a deleted item shows `detached` with who removed it, and a note never notifies, opens an ask or counts in Needs you; each note is recorded as `note.opened` and `note.closed`, which feed the `notes` projection the return card and the editor panel (#180) read
- Builds inside #1453: the wrapper opens from a card and closes back to it. It isn't a window or a tab of its own

### Fields
**[Note](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#note)**
- `{note: ULID, doc, item: ID, rev: u64, t: flick (optional), region: {x, y, w, h}, u (optional), text: string}` (`rev`: the revision you saw; `t`: the frame's time; `region`: a rectangle of that frame)
- Writer: you, from the connection, with your input's serial in the editor panel the app ships or your click on a return card
- `state: open | detached | closed`; closed with `{by: you | check, rev, run}`
- It can never: Be written, edited or closed by an agent or a plug-in; close on a writer's word; change the document; answer an ask

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An agent-made HTML page that fetches a remote script or posts a form makes no network request when opened from the card
- [ ] On a test agent's chart drawn on its return card you leave the note "Q3's label covers Q4's" on the Q3 label, and the agent's session receives exactly one send-back item carrying the note's ID, the label's ID, the revision you saw and your text. Its next revision moves the label 2 px and its stop says fixed; a test canvas module's rule that flags labels overlapping each other still finds the two labels overlapping, so the note stays open on that stop's card, naming that rule's issue. A revision that moves the label clear with every document check passing closes it with `by: check`, naming that revision and the run. A planted rule that closes a note on the agent's stop, or on any revision that changes the item, fails on the 2 px revision, naming the note
- [ ] Every deep_* tool a test agent calls naming the note's ID, and every module a test plug-in calls, fails to write, edit or close a note, naming the call, and the record shows no note event from either; once the agent deletes the Q3 label, the note shows `detached` naming the agent and the revision and stays open until you close it; and leaving or closing a note changes neither the Needs-you count nor any notification
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of a chart on a return card with a note on the Q3 label, and an agent HTML page in its wrapper, taken by the check run from the app at the reference window, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it

### Proof
The Q3 label note through each revision, every agent and plug-in write refused, and the HTML page making no request.

A linked test counts only when run against our output (#136). Without a runner the lane is BLOCKED with one unblock ask.

The card drawn for each return from the record: what changed, the verdict line, what needs you and the proof, with plug-in actions read from their records and the planted cards that make return.card@1.

**Epic:** #241 · **Part of:** #145 · **Design:** [First-party extensions that ship on by default](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#first-party-extensions-that-ship-on-by-default) · [Projections the canvas reads](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#projections-the-canvas-reads) · [Blocks for plug-ins that do real work](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#blocks-for-plug-ins-that-do-real-work) · [The event catalogue](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#the-event-catalogue) · [Closed enums](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/canvas-primitives.md#closed-enums)

### Scope
- A return for every stop that did work, asked something, answered a prompt a person typed, or ended early (says done, asks, answers, stopped or interrupted), kept as a projection of the record
- The card, top to bottom: what changed in one plain sentence from the summary template; the verdict line, or "says done" with the checks still running and their expected time; what needs you, as the stop's questions sorted by kind, each answered on its question card in a slot the card reserves; the proof, the screenshot at the step a check looked at beside the end state with its highlight strip; the definition's deliverables with their size and digest, opened from a copy kept by hash so they still open after the worktree is gone, shown as work products and never as proof; then what the agent drew
- A return with nothing for you folds to one line, such as "PASS 4/4 · receipt"; an answer stays open; and only a return with an ask notifies you
- The same card shows on the session's page, in the box's thread, and in any channel that can draw it; a channel that can't shows the summary and a link back
- Its planted cards form `return.card@1`, with the turn view's (#198): the kit a view that replaces the return card passes at install in a replica (#60)
- What changed includes each plug-in action the session called before the stop, from its `action.entered` and `action.reported` records: a no-op reads "no change", and a false or unverified change, or a call never reported, says so ahead of anything the agent wrote; the agent's words never fill it
- On a session's page, the line tab shows the newest return card open under the line, and earlier returns folded to one line each, newest first, above the box
- A folded return also says how long its turn worked and how many tool calls it made, such as "worked 3 min · 7 steps", from the turn's prompt and stop events in the record and the tool events between them, never from the agent's text
- The proof section reads each requirement that didn't pass in three parts: what you asked, in the words the requirement was approved in; what happened, as its result sentence (#938); and how it stands against the code before the change: "broke in this change" (a FAIL on a check the base passed), "already failing before this change" (BLOCKED as inherited, with its fix task), or "couldn't be checked" with what's missing and who can supply it (BLOCKED for a cause outside the code, or INCONCLUSIVE with the runs still needed). The state word and its glyph stay as States people see sets them
- A return whose verdict is PASS carries one control, "Not right", with an optional sentence, "What should have happened?", and plain reason chips: not what I asked, looks broken, made something up, didn't finish. It records an escape after PASS naming that verdict, as a revert does (#334); opens a fix task whose definition is drafted blind from your sentence (#335); counts as a pass you reopened as broken (#118, #722); and adds the task to the replay set (#112). It raises no ask and never goes to the session that made the claim as its instruction
- Under #1453: at rest a card shows what changed, the verdict line, what needs you and the proof, and the other sections open from it. A folded return draws one line, and its "worked 3 min · 7 steps" stays in the row's accessible name and on the opened card

- [ ] Jumping to a past return shows the same card as when it arrived, replayed from the record
- [ ] A deliverable still opens from the card after its worktree is deleted, and its digest matches the definition's record

How an extension improves: its uses recorded on your machine become proposed changes your agent builds, with a rule offered after three alike, patches kept over published packages, and suggestions from patterns in the record.

**Epic:** #6 · **Part of:** #59 · **Design:** [Extension API (TypeScript, in-process)](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#extension-api-typescript-in-process) · [The learned layer](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#the-learned-layer)

### Scope
- Improves with use: how each extension is used (opens, dismissals, undos, errors, gestures) is recorded on your machine only; a pattern becomes a proposed change in plain words, your agent builds it, and it is replayed against your recorded uses
- A change that alters a past result is held for you; after three approved changes alike inside the access you already granted, it offers a rule, and with your yes later ones apply on their own; every change is in the learned-layer history and can be rolled back; new access always asks
- An improvement to a package someone else published is a patch layer over its pinned version; an update proposes each patch again against the new version, and a patch that no longer applies waits for you
- Suggestions: from patterns in the record, such as the same question asked of agents again and again, DeepBuild offers a gadget or a tab (the hub counts exact repeats; anything fuzzier is a reading job in your own agent, on your plan); your agent builds it in a copy first and only one that passes the checks is shown; a suggestion never counts as an ask, one shows at a time, adding it takes one tap, and Not now mutes it for a month
- Refused calls count among an extension's uses: its origin shows its `capability.refused` events as one counted series per grant clause, and a proposed change or its removal cites them
- A suggestion never shows while you have words queued in a session's box, and none comes from a subagent's turn or a plug-in's call: only the hub's exact-repeat count and your own agent's reading job propose one

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An improvement that changes any recorded result is held for you; one that needs new access is always an ask
- [ ] A suggestion never counts in Needs you, is never built when the plan window is down to the reserve, and asks before any access beyond reading what you already granted
- [ ] A fourth improvement like three you approved is held unless you accepted the rule it offered, and new access always asks
- [ ] With three of your agent's improvements applied over a published stocks package at 1.0.0, updating it to 1.1.0 proposes each patch again against 1.1.0: the two that still apply are proposed again, the one whose lines 1.1.0 changed waits for you, and none runs before your yes; an updater that keeps your patched files over 1.1.0, or drops the patches, fails this test, naming the patch
- [ ] The hub finds only exact repeats; any other pattern is found by a reading job in your own agent, on your plan
- [ ] A stocks extension that tries 400 times overnight to reach a host it never declared shows one series on its origin, 400 calls refused for that host, and the next proposed change, or its removal, cites that series; an origin that ignores refusal events shows nothing and fails this test
- [ ] With two follow-ups queued in a session's box, a ready suggestion waits and shows once the queue is empty; a suggestion proposed from a subagent's turn is dropped and recorded, naming the turn

### Proof
One improvement replayed on recorded uses, an update proposing patches again, and one suggestion from the pattern to the tap that adds it.

Each task's definition of done drafted apart from the working session and checked on the base commit, so every requirement names what would refute it. The kernel then locks it.

**Epic:** #5 · **Part of:** #50 · **Design:** [First-party extensions that ship on by default](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#first-party-extensions-that-ship-on-by-default) · [How runs become one of five verdicts](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#how-runs-become-one-of-five-verdicts) · [What done means, fixed at the start](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#what-done-means-fixed-at-the-start)

### Scope
- Drafts each task's definition of done at its start (#81), in a job separate from the working session, from the ask, the base commit and your wiki (your proof bar included), never from the working session; the kernel then locks it
- Drafting starts on issue links, issue branch names and prompts that ask for new or changed behavior; the triggers are tuned on the transcript archive
- Each drafted requirement names the observation that would refute it; one left without a check lists the existing checks that came closest, why each falls short, and the search behind them; new behavior gets its check through the entry point the issue or the spec names, such as a command, a route or a journey, so it runs on the base commit and fails there on its assertion
- Each drafted check names in `asserts` the assertions that carry its requirement, never a setup or helper assertion; a journey asserts with an `expect` that each element the new behavior adds is shown before it acts on one, and a fix for a crash names an assertion that catches it, such as `expect(() => f([])).not.toThrow()`
- On a base with nothing to start (no start command for the service a check enters, no binary or package script for its command, no package for its module), `deep` builds the declared surface as a program that does nothing (#31) and the check must fail on it on a named assertion; it is then kept with `stand_in` set, its receipt line says 'proven on a stand-in', and proof-bar requirements that compare with the base cover only what the base has
- When a definition needs a journey, the job drives a stack started from the base checkout, as a base run's is (#36, #580), with no model, to check each locator it writes against the running app before the check's base run; it reads only the base commit, a job that can't start that stack drafts from the code alone and says so on the definition, and a base with nothing to start has no such stack. Where it can't know a journey's controls, because the repo has no test IDs or the screen is new, it locates each element by what the issue says of it, and an element the issue leaves unnamed goes to the early question; goal steps (#581) aren't built in week 5, since #573's readings didn't show they help
- A requirement about computed numbers, such as a kernel's output, gets a drafted check with a numeric contract (#28) whose tolerance comes from the issue or the approved spec; a tolerance neither states goes to the early question. Its fixtures add the inputs where wrong math hides behind plausible output: values near the edge of the accumulation type's range and reductions long enough that a narrower accumulator drifts past the tolerance; masked, empty and length-one inputs, such as a fully masked row or an empty batch; and inputs where two selections disagree, such as a batch that mixes prefill and decode lengths so every block path runs, a length that leaves the last block partly filled, or tied scores
- A drafted check enters only through a surface the issue or the approved spec names (a command, route, page, module or message text it states) and asserts only what they state. Where the issue leaves the interface open, such as a message's exact wording, a data shape, an element's accessible name, when a retry runs, or which of two remedies it allows, the job drafts no check that guesses: the requirement goes to the early question, which names what was left open, and its check is drafted from the answer. In #573, 20 of 42 drafted checks failed on the base where they should and then failed on the merged fix: 17 asserted something their issue doesn't state, and the other 3 asserted what it states and still failed (a label matched exactly, ambiguous wording read the other way, a key the issue names that the base's code names differently), which is what a dispute with `deep_propose` is for
- A requirement drawn from an acceptance criterion quotes it in full, since its checks are written from the requirement's text, and each condition the criterion states is named in its checks' `asserts`. In #573, two raters agreed the drafted requirements stated only 65 of 108 criteria in full; in 23 more, a requirement quoted or paraphrased its criterion but dropped a condition it states
- The stand-in for a base with nothing to start and the early question are this task's main path, built and tested first, not edge cases: in #573, 55 of 108 requirements for new or fixed behavior got no check because the code a check would enter wasn't on the base yet
- The job's own base run of each drafted check happens the way the gate's will: in a fresh temporary checkout of the base from #31, never the job's own folder, holding none of the job's files but the check's, and through the repo's own test entry, its build first where the test script runs one. In #573, eight checks in three issues ran only because of build output the job had left in its checkout
- The readings (#45) count checks for behavior that must not change, the guards, apart from new-behavior checks: new-behavior checks as kept, kept on a stand-in, dropped for passing on the base, dropped for failing elsewhere, and sent to the early question; guards as kept or dropped for failing on the base. In #573, all 12 checks dropped for passing on the base were guards behaving as the design asks
- A held-out twin's expected output never enters the run: the run gets the twin's input and writes its output where the runner names, and the runner compares it with the expected output outside the run, by the check's declared comparison (equality, or its numeric contract). A check whose comparison lives only in its test code gets no twin, and its definition says so
- A requirement that says the same input gives the same output is drafted as a check that runs the code twice, in two processes, and compares both outputs whole
- Each drafted definition names the task's kind of issue and its plan (the files and parts it expects to touch), which the done gate's size and scope check reads (#324); today that check gets them only from a handed fixture

### Fields
**[Definition of done](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#definition-of-done)**
- `{task_ref, requirements: [{id, text, source_line, refuted_by, check, on_base, asserts, stand_in, depth, oracle, near_misses}], deliverables, issue_rev, base_commit, hash, budget}`. A job that sees only the ask and the base commit drafts it, and then it's locked. Every attempt on the task shares it. Each requirement names the observation that would refute it, so it can fail. A requirement left without a check lists the existing checks that came closest, why each falls short, and the search behind them. Each requirement also says what its check must do on the base commit: `on_base: fails` for new or fixed behavior, `passes` for behavior that must not change. The base-commit rule reads that field, never the requirement's wording. `asserts` lists the assertions in its check that carry the requirement: each expect or assert line by file and line, a journey's end-state check by its step ID, or a test's deadline where the requirement is about time, never a setup or helper assertion. The definition's hash covers them, and on the base a failure counts only at one of them. `stand_in` is set only when a program that does nothing stood in for the base: it names the surface the check enters through and the stand-in's hash.
- It can never: Be drafted from the agent's own work

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A requirement left without a check lists at least one near-miss check and why it falls short, or says none exists, with its search
- [ ] A drafted check that runs nothing on the base commit, or behaves the wrong way there (one for new or fixed behavior passes, or fails anywhere but an assertion its definition names, or one for unchanged behavior fails), is dropped, and its requirement becomes the early question, after one redraft when it failed elsewhere
- [ ] The drafting job's inputs are only the ask, the repo at the base commit, the approved spec and feature map, and your wiki as it stood at session start, plus, when a definition needs a journey, a stack started from the base checkout; a test shows the working session's transcript, diff, worktree and stack never reach it
- [ ] A drafted definition whose new checks each behave right on the base commit, with nothing in it of taste and no text from anyone but you or a repo collaborator, counts without an ask and shows under Decided for you with an overrule
- [ ] Budgets, on the reference Mac in the local preflight, compared with the merge base: drafting each task's definition stays within its stated plan share
- [ ] Each drafted check with a fixture also gets held-out twins made from that fixture by the same generator with another seed, or by a transform that must not change the answer (renamed IDs, a shifted time, a mirrored scene, an extra row), kept where the working session can't read them, and the gate runs every twin with its check: a planted fix that returns the visible fixture's expected value for its exact input passes the visible check and fails its renamed-ID twin, so the claim is FAIL naming the check, a read of a twin from the session is denied, and the send-back never quotes a twin's input

A base-run filter that counts any failed test as proof keeps the `TypeError` check and fails this test, naming it
- [ ] On the sample app's base build, a drafted Playwright check that fails at its named `expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Export' })).toBeVisible()` by a locator timeout is kept; one that times out at `click()` on that button before any expect, one whose API client throws on a 404 before its first step, and one that reads `fixtures/export.json`, which the base lacks, are each dropped, naming the failure's file and line. A redraft that also fails elsewhere sends the requirement to the early question, and a check that passes on the base gets no redraft. A job that asks before redrafting, or redrafts more than once, fails this test

The one way an agent changes a spec: a proposal that runs with its evidence attached and waits for your approval, and a masked check refused at once.

**Epic:** #5 · **Part of:** #50 · **Design:** [First-party extensions that ship on by default](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#first-party-extensions-that-ship-on-by-default) · [Threats, and what stops each one](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#threats-and-what-stops-each-one) · [How runs become one of five verdicts](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#how-runs-become-one-of-five-verdicts)

### Scope
- `deep_propose`: agents propose a check, a journey or a feature entry, and the done gate asks the agent that changed a feature with no journey to propose one. A proposal runs at once with its evidence attached, and decides nothing until it's approved
- A tolerance only tightens: a change to a check's numeric contract (#28) that raises a bound or narrows the accumulation type is refused, even with your approval, and so is a waiver of a failure inside the looser bound. A looser contract lands only as a new check with its own ID, proposed with the old and new contracts and runs of both on the same inputs, before and after the change that needs it; once you approve it, it replaces the old check for later claims, the verdicts made on the old one stay as they were, and each receipt line that counts it says its tolerance was loosened, from what and when
- A check proposed because work slipped past the checks that passed it, an escape after PASS such as a revert or a follow-up fix, names that verdict, and it can be approved only once it fails, at an assertion it names, on the commit the escaped verdict passed. Once approved, it runs once over the code already in, on the default branch's head in a temporary checkout (#31) and in the slow lane: each failure there becomes an inherited fix task, one per cause, counted as an escape the check found (#45). Those runs are new evidence, and no verdict already made changes
- An issue proposed from an attempt inside a work run (#1011) records that attempt and joins the run's one batched authority ask, never an ask of its own; it changes nothing in the run until you approve its row
- `deep_propose` is on main as a learned-layer proposal (`propose` in `packages/hub/src/core.ts`, the tool in `packages/hub/src/tools.ts`): it records `learn.proposed`, raises a choice ask and runs nothing. This task changes that tool for a check, a journey or a feature entry: the proposal runs at once, and the gate's masked-exit rule refuses a masked command before any ask. A proposal of another target, such as a wiki claim or a rule, keeps today's path
- A known failure is waived the same way: an agent proposes a waiver of one check's exact error text with `deep_propose`, with an owner and an end date or the condition that ends it (#28). It decides nothing until you approve it, and never by the agent whose claim it would cover. Once approved, the core records it and the gate hands it to the verdict engine at every later claim, so what it covers shows as unwatched while it lasts

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A drafted or proposed check changes no verdict until it's approved, and agents still can't write `.deepbuild/`
- [ ] An agent that changes a feature with no journey is asked to propose one, and the proposal reaches Needs you
- [ ] An agent's `deep_propose` of the check `npm test || true` is refused at once, naming "exit status masked by `|| true`", and nothing reaches Needs you; the same proposal as `npm test` runs with its evidence attached
- [ ] A spec check with contract `{atol: 1e-3, rtol: 1e-3}` edited in place to `atol: 1e-2` is refused even with your approval, naming the raised bound, and a waiver of a failure whose largest error is 5e-3 is refused the same way. The same loosening proposed as a new check, with both contracts and runs of each on the same inputs before and after the change, lands once you approve it: later claims count only the new check, the verdicts made on the old one are unchanged, and the new check's receipt line says its tolerance was loosened from 1e-3 to 1e-2 and when. A guard that lets the approved in-place edit through, or that refuses the new check too, fails this test
- [ ] A check proposed for a reverted change, naming that change's PASS verdict, can't be approved while it passes on that verdict's commit, and can once it fails there at its named assertion. Once approved, it runs once on the default branch's head, where it fails in two places with two causes: two inherited fix tasks open before any claim touches that code, the readings count two escapes the check found, and every earlier verdict row is unchanged. A gate that runs the new check only at the next claim opens no fix task before it, and one that rewrites the earlier PASS changes a verdict row, and each fails this test, naming the task or the verdict
- [ ] An agent's `deep_propose` of a waiver for a check's exact error text decides nothing until you approve it: the next claim whose only failure on that check is that error stays FAIL. Once you approve it, the next such claim reads that check INCONCLUSIVE, naming the waived error as unwatched, and a different failure on the same check still fails. A gate that hands the verdict engine no waivers leaves the approved case FAIL and fails this test
- [ ] An approved waiver past its end date leaves the next such claim FAIL, naming the error

### Proof
An agent's proposal reaching Needs you with its evidence, and a masked proposal refused naming the mask, each shown failing first.

### Depends on
- #333 Spec drafting: the checks a repo already runs, each run once with masked ones left out, and one approval per repo
- #26 MCP server: ask, wait, open items, status and search
- #31 Base-commit runs in a temporary checkout from DeepBuild's object store

The gate runner (#29) checks each claim against its ask's locked definition and makes a claim for each ask a stop touched, but the records it reads, the asks, their tasks and the lock, sat in #81, which waited on the done gate (#32), which waits on the gate runner. Put the kernel's part of ask-tasks ahead of the gate; #81 keeps the flow around drafting.

**Epic:** #2 · **Design:** [What done means, fixed at the start](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#what-done-means-fixed-at-the-start) · [The contract (kernel)](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#the-contract-kernel) · [Ask-task](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#ask-task) · [Definition of done](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#definition-of-done) · [Threats, and what stops each one](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#threats-and-what-stops-each-one)

### Scope
- `user.ask` events for every prompt and every message typed while the agent works, each with its `from` (person, scheduled, subagent, session or continuation) from the prompt's recorded origin, so only a prompt a person typed is your ask
- Each ask that asks for new or changed behavior opens a task under the session's thread, keyed by an issue or a message handle (`session:id#msg`)
- Its definition is locked as `definition.locked`, with its hash, the issue's revision and the base commit; every attempt on the task shares it, and it changes after the lock only through a dispute you answer. The kernel locks the definition it is handed (a fixture in this task's tests, the issue's criteria from week 3, the drafted one from week 5) and never drafts one
- Each requirement keeps the author of the text it came from, with the role its work source's `work.item@1` reading gives that author, never a role read from the text: text from anyone but you or a repo collaborator can add requirements, never remove or waive one, and an issue that carries such text locks its definition only after one ask about it
- A session's first prompt and a message typed mid-turn open a task only when they ask for new or changed behavior, like a later prompt; one that only asks a question opens no task and no drafting job, and a stop that only answers it is an answer, which the stop rule doesn't judge
- The stop and answer rule, which the gate runner (#29) and the stop judge (#82) cite and neither restates: a stop right after startup, a resume or `/clear`, or an answer to a prompt you typed, is never a claim; an answer is a stop whose turn began with a prompt a person typed that opened no task, with no edit, write or ask in the turn
- An issue that carries outsider text locks at once, without that text. The return card says in one line what was left out and from whom, with Add it, which is your own change to the definition. Outsider text still can't remove or waive a requirement. This replaces "locks its definition only after one ask about it" above, and the criterion that pins the wait goes through its blind redraft (Nov 9 call)

### Fields
**[Ask-task](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#ask-task)**
- Something you asked for, with its own definition of done: `{task_ref, thread, definition, state, owner}`. Its `task_ref` is an issue or a message handle such as `session:id#msg`. A long session holds many.
- It can never: Close before its check passes, or change its definition after the lock except through a dispute you answer

**[Definition of done](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#definition-of-done)**
- `{task_ref, requirements: [{id, text, source_line, refuted_by, check, depth, oracle, near_misses}], deliverables, issue_rev, base_commit, hash, budget}`. A job that sees only the ask and the base commit drafts it, and then it's locked. Every attempt on the task shares it. Each requirement names the observation that would refute it, so it can fail. A requirement left without a check lists the existing checks that came closest, why each falls short, and the search behind them.
- It can never: Be drafted from the agent's own work

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A session with three asks over three days holds three locked definitions
- [ ] A message typed mid-turn that asks for new or changed behavior becomes a task within one hook
- [ ] A rename-only prompt opens no task
- [ ] Definitions survive a resume and a compaction
- [ ] An issue comment from an account outside the repo that says "skip the e2e test" leaves that requirement in the definition, marks its author on what it added, and the definition waits for one answer before it locks; the author's role comes from the comment's `work.item@1` reading, here a test source's (the GitHub source's is #32's, which tests it on GitHub issues), so the same comment signed "the repo owner" in its text still waits, and a lock that reads the role from the text fails this test
- [ ] A `/loop` iteration, a background subagent's report and a message from another Claude Code session each fire UserPromptSubmit, and none opens an ask, a task or a drafting job; each is recorded with its `from`
- [ ] A session whose first prompt is "explain how the auth middleware checks expiry" opens no task and starts no drafting job, its `user.ask` recording `tasks: []`, and a session whose first prompt is "make the auth middleware reject expired tokens" opens one task; a planted rule that opens a task for every first prompt fails on the first, naming its message handle
- [ ] Typed while the agent works, "why did you pick bcrypt?" opens no task, and "also add a test for expired tokens" opens one within one hook; a planted rule that opens a task for every mid-turn message fails on the first, naming its message handle
- [ ] Each `definition.locked` carries the definition's hash, the issue's revision and the base commit, and one without any of them fails its schema, naming the field; the hash recomputed from the locked definition equals the recorded one, and a requirement edited in the store after the lock gives another; a planted lock that hashes only the requirement IDs gives the same hash after the edit and fails this test, naming the requirement
- [ ] On recorded turns, the stop rule reads a stop right after startup, one right after a resume, one right after `/clear`, and one whose turn began with your typed question that opened no task and only read two files, each as no claim, and the same question's turn with one edit in it as a claim; a planted rule that reads every stop with tool calls as a claim fails on the question, naming the stop
- [ ] Budgets, on the reference Mac in the local preflight, compared with the merge base: turning a message into a task adds under 5 ms to the prompt hook
- [ ] A drafted check file under `.deepbuild/` changed after the lock by a write the guard didn't recognize makes the next claim's recomputed hash differ from the locked one: the claim's checks run the approved bytes kept by digest in the hub, and the change becomes a proposal naming the file; a lock that hashes requirement records with check paths but not their bytes gives the same hash and fails this test
- [ ] An outside account's comment that adds "also support Windows" leaves the definition locked without it and raises no ask. The return card names the comment and its author, and Add it puts the requirement in as yours. A planted lock that takes the outsider's requirement in fails, naming the author

Every piece that holds a real-time arena game writes the same core again in its own logic: a character controller over the level's boxes and ramps, projectiles and their hits, a grid of paint over the level's surfaces that the rules read, and bots that aim with a reaction time and walk the navigation graph. Each is a place to go wrong, and nothing first-party proves any of it. An arena action kit, a blueprint like the grid core kit (#197), would ship them as linked libraries with fixtures whose answers come from first principles, with its own checks and a recipe. It reopens the lines that complete-game kits beyond the grid core wait, genre layers no brief has asked for yet among them (Cut, or deferred), that each genre layer waits for a brief of its genre (Decided: Kits), and that a complete game takes the engine project route (Not proposed, and why; Decided: Bounded games on the canvas), so it needs your decision. Tracked, not scheduled: the line it reopens stands until you decide, and it starts when a piece needs it.

- [ ] A room that starts with two players and two empty seats (#278) has arena.bots play the empty seats from step 0, and a seat handed to a bot mid-match (#277) is played by arena.bots from the next confirmed step, with every copy's full-state hashes equal; a match's stamps reach the paint layer (#263) as occurrences, and a rollback drops the stamps of the steps it replaces

Many services a live view reads, and outside code wikis, answer over MCP. #102 plans non-HTTP sources; this adds MCP as one of them, with what MCP needs beyond HTTP: a server's session, tools counted as read and a sandboxed local server. An extension can't add it, because a plug-in makes no outside call itself and every call goes through capabilities in the hub. The same holds for plug-ins' runner jobs, which may use MCP servers only inside the plug-in's own grant.

**Epic:** #6 · **Design:** [Blocks for plug-ins that do real work](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#blocks-for-plug-ins-that-do-real-work) · [Extension API (TypeScript, in-process)](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#extension-api-typescript-in-process) · [Threats, and what stops each one](https://github.com/windoliver/deepbuild/blob/main/docs/technical-design.md#threats-and-what-stops-each-one)

### Scope
- A source may be one tool on an MCP server: a remote server at a URL whose host the grant names, over streamable HTTP, or a local stdio server, a command the manifest names, that the supervisor starts in the platform sandbox (#236) under the plug-in's grant and a run token; the hub holds the session and makes every call, with the same quota, timeout, cache and cost record
- The hub records the server's tool list at install, at each session it opens with the server and on the server's list-changed notice, with each tool's schema digest, as for every agent's servers on the guard path (#321), and checks it before the first call after any of these; it calls only a tool counted as read by a facts entry or your decision on the trusted path (#304), never by the server's hints or the tool's name; an unknown tool counts as change, and a decision about a tool lapses when its schema changes
- A schedule run whose every call the hub's own quota refuses is INCONCLUSIVE, as a provider's rate limit is, and one that recorded readings passes on them; the schedule holds until the time the quota gives
- A structured result maps through the source's schema: a number with a unit, or a value from a closed list the schema names, is a reading. Readings gain an `outside` mark: free text, any field the schema doesn't type, and everything from a source that its manifest declares outside, or that you mark outside in its approval sentence, are shown with their source and age, no check, verdict, notice or map row cites them, and none fills an extension's hook context; map layers attach them to rows as text (#259)
- A secret reaches a remote server by handle, as a header on its host, and a local one through `deep mcp-exec` (#148); never in a config file, a URL, a log, the record or a prompt, and scrubbed from results as for HTTP sources. A remote server that signs in with OAuth uses the sources' OAuth loopback (#102)
- Outside text, from an outside code wiki or a model job, attaches to a row as a reading marked outside, shown in its panel with its source and age; it adds, removes and moves no row, and no check cites it. None is on by default, and for a repo that isn't public the approval sentence says the provider must hold a copy of its code
- A plug-in's runner job may name MCP servers inside the plug-in's own grant: a remote server is a host the grant names, and a local one runs sandboxed under the plug-in's grant, never as the copy synced to your agents. The runner lists only those servers, with only their tools counted as read, in the job's own MCP config; PreToolUse denies any other tool as a second guard; what a tool returns is filtered by the grant; and the approval sentence names each server with the access it brings

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A test source over streamable HTTP calls a recorded server's `list_services` tool every 30 s, with a 60 s freshness; `list_services` counts as read only by a facts entry or your decision, and before either the source is BLOCKED; a host that takes the `list_` name or a `readOnlyHint` as read calls it and fails, naming the tool
- [ ] Once counted as read, its structured result maps into readings with unit, source and as-of time; a recorded answer missing a required field makes no reading, and the value grays 60 s after the last good answer's as-of time
- [ ] A recorded result `{service: "api", rate: 40, unit: "1/s", status: "up", note: "fine"}`, under a schema that keys it by `service`, takes `unit` as rate's unit and types status as one of up or down, gives two readings for `api`, rate and status, and one reading marked outside, note; a host that lets a notice cite note fails, naming the field
- [ ] A source that names `get_rate`, not yet counted, is BLOCKED, naming the tool, and makes no call; once you count it as read, it runs; when the recorded server's next session lists `get_rate` with a changed input schema, your decision lapses and the source is BLOCKED again, with no call, until you decide again; a host that keeps calling after the schema change fails, naming the tool
- [ ] A text-only result becomes a reading marked outside that a panel shows with its source and age; a notice that cites it is refused, naming the reading, and a check that cites it is INVALID
- [ ] A planted `map.layer@1` fill whose rows cite only an outside reading is refused with the layer's code `unsupported`, naming each row and the citation
- [ ] A local stdio server starts under the supervisor with a run token and the plug-in's grant; a planted server whose tool fetches `cdn.other.example` once per call is refused, with one `capability.refused` event per call naming the host; the call makes no reading, and the source's value grays once it passes its freshness
- [ ] With #102's test key `mk/test+51f0c9=` by handle for a remote server, the value reaches only that host's request header; it appears in no config file, URL, log, record entry or evidence, in any of #102's scrub forms, and a planted server that echoes it back has it scrubbed before the plug-in reads the result; a local server gets the value only through `deep mcp-exec`, in its own process, never on its command line, in a file or in the record
- [ ] With a quota of 10 calls a minute and a schedule that reads it every 1 s on a test clock from 10:00:00 to 10:02:59, a source over MCP makes exactly 10 calls in each of the minutes 10:00, 10:01 and 10:02, 30 in all; each run the quota refuses appends one `capability.refused` naming the quota and ends INCONCLUSIVE, never FAIL, and the schedule never pauses
- [ ] A host that skips the quota for MCP sources makes 180 calls in those three minutes, and one that counts the refusals as FAIL pauses the schedule after 10 calls; each fails, naming the count
- [ ] With two servers, `wiki`, a local command in the plug-in's manifest, and `metrics`, synced to your agents but outside the plug-in's grant, a job that names `wiki` gets only `wiki` and only its tools counted as read: in a recorded run whose agent tries `wiki`'s `update_page`, counted as change, and `metrics`'s `get_rate`, the recorded servers receive neither call, and the job's tool list holds only `wiki`'s tools counted as read; with a planted runner config that also lists `metrics`, PreToolUse denies `get_rate`, naming the tool, and `metrics` still receives no call; its approval sentence names `wiki`
- [ ] A manifest that names `metrics` for a job is refused at install, naming the server; a runner that hands the job your agents' synced set lets `get_rate` reach `metrics` and fails, naming the server
- [ ] A plug-in granted one host names a local file server for its job; the job's read of a planted `~/.ssh/config` in the test's temporary home, outside the grant, returns nothing and appends a `capability.refused` event naming the path; a runner that starts the server with your full access returns the file and fails, naming the path
- [ ] Budgets, on the reference Mac in the local preflight, compared with the merge base: an MCP source call adds under 10 ms beyond the server's answer, and one session serves every call while the server keeps it
- [ ] A row with outside text shows it in its panel with its source and age; turning the source off removes the text and no row, and a check that cites the outside text is INVALID, naming the reading
- [ ] On a fresh install no outside text source is on, and the fixture repo's map draws in full; turning on a recorded code wiki for a private fixture repo shows one approval sentence that names the provider's host and says it must hold a copy of the repo's code, and nothing is sent before your yes; a host that sends before the yes, or leaves the copy out of the sentence for a private repo, fails, naming the source
- [ ] Shown to you: screenshots of the fixture repo's map with a service layer, a reading grayed after 60 s and a panel showing an outside reading with its source and age, taken by the check run from the app at the reference window, are attached to the PR and shown to you in the session. Whether they look right is one taste call, recorded; without it the run stays INCONCLUSIVE, never PASS, and no criterion above reads a picture to judge it
